summary: Round 2 addresses both round-1 minors. Fix 1: Test_helpTemplate_pauseEntry now asserts entry[descColumn(entry):] equals the exact expected description text, deliberately not the raw first line. This is sound, not a weaker substitute: the implementer's reasoning holds — a raw-line literal would bake the 13-space padding into the assertion and break on any future block-wide re-indentation, which is precisely the drift the computed-column alignment check exists to tolerate. Verified by mutation myself: 'need'->'require' fails the new assertion (and separately trips the >80-column check, since 'require' is longer). Verified the description-slice form has no coverage hole: reducing the internal padding by one space (key stays at column 5, description shifts to column 22) is still caught, by the pre-existing assert.Equal(descColumn(scroll), descColumn(entry)) alignment check, independent of the new wording assertion. So column drift and wording drift are each covered by one of the two assertions; together they leave no gap a raw-line literal would have closed. Fix 2: the Test_helpTemplate_formatVerbs comment was rewritten (2 lines removed, 6 added, +11/-2 total including the 5-line addition in fix 1) with no assertion removed or weakened — confirmed by diff and by test count (still 4 assertions, both fixes are comment/assertion additions only). Re-ran both mutations myself: a bare stray '%' still fails at the go-vet/build stage before any test assertion executes ('fmt.Fprintf format %, has unknown verb ,' — build failed), and a doubled '%%' still passes go vet cleanly (exit 0) while failing this test's strings.Count assertions (3 vs 1, 2 vs 1). The new comment states exactly this — it does not overclaim (still says vet catches ordinary stray verbs harder/earlier) and does not underclaim (still credits the test with the %% case, which I re-confirmed vet does not catch). Full helpTemplate test run (-race -count=5) is green and stable. top/help.go is untouched (byte-identical to cd542da, confirmed via git show). No new findings.
